## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{10}{95}{10}{10}{10}{10}
\end{marginfigure}

_*How do we compile runtime knowledge and schemas directly into model weights without destroying general reasoning?*_

When an agent system begins operation, its knowledge of tool definitions, formatting schemas, repository idioms, and domain protocols is supplied dynamically as text within the prompt context window. While flexible, this approach incurs a heavy Systems Prompt Tax: every single model invocation re-evaluates thousands of tokens of static instructions, consuming accelerator memory, increasing Time to First Token (TTFT) latency, and occupying space that should be reserved for active task state. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and knowledge distillation act as a policy compiler: translating verbose, in-context runtime instructions into dense neural parameters. Once compiled into weights, the model reliably emits exact JSON schemas, invokes specialized tools, and adheres to complex operational workflows with minimal prompt scaffolding. Yet supervised adaptation introduces a treacherous systems trade-off: catastrophic forgetting. Aggressively training a model on narrow tool-calling syntax frequently repurposes the very attention circuits responsible for general reasoning, mathematical deduction, and code comprehension. An agent engineering team must approach fine-tuning with the rigor of compiler optimization: formalizing context compilation, selecting parameter-efficient adaptation strategies (LoRA, distillation), curating regularization anchor sets to prevent catastrophic forgetting, and validating specialized agent policies across regression suites.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Model the Systems Prompt Tax, quantifying the latency, memory, and financial cost savings achieved by compiling static context instructions into model weights.
- Deconstruct the loss formulations for Supervised Fine-Tuning across multi-turn agent trajectories, masking user prompts and tool observations to compute loss strictly on model action tokens.
- Evaluate parameter-efficient fine-tuning architectures (LoRA, QLoRA) versus full-parameter fine-tuning, analyzing memory footprints, compute budgets, and parameter merging overheads.
- Analyze the mechanics of catastrophic forgetting during domain specialization, designing replay buffers and KL-divergence regularization strategies to preserve general reasoning.
- Implement knowledge distillation pipelines that compress complex reasoning trajectories from expensive teacher frontier models into compact, low-latency student models.
- Establish comprehensive pre-release regression suites to verify that fine-tuned policies maintain instruction-following fidelity, tool syntax compliance, and general problem-solving capabilities.

:::

## Trajectory Example Serialization {#sec-vol3-sft-serialization}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**

### The Serialization Contract

An agent trajectory during online execution exists as a distributed, asynchronous event trace recorded within an Agent Control Block (ACB). The ACB captures heterogeneous operational records: user instructions delivered over network sockets, system configuration directives, internal reasoning tokens emitted by the model, structured RPC invocations to external tools, and raw observational payloads returned by the runtime environment. To compile these asynchronous event logs into a dataset suitable for autoregressive supervised adaptation, the data pipeline must execute a deterministic serialization contract. This contract converts discrete, typed event records into a single contiguous token sequence governed by explicit, immutable role boundaries.

Standard chat-completion formats fail to represent agent trajectories because they assume a simple alternating dialogue between user and assistant. A robust agent serialization specification requires four non-overlapping role partitions:

1. `System`: Immutable operational parameters, global behavioral policies, and formal tool schemas defining the tool execution interface.
2. `User`: External task descriptions, runtime constraints, and mid-trajectory steering interventions.
3. `Assistant`: Model-generated tokens partitioned strictly into internal deliberative rationales and executable tool-call specifications.
4. `Environment`: Observation payloads produced by tool execution runtimes, operating system shells, API gateways, or external sensors.

Each partition must be framed by dedicated control tokens (for example, `<|start_user|>` and `<|end_user|>`, or `<|start_env|>` and `<|end_env|>`). These control tokens are not natural language strings; they are single atomic tokens reserved in the tokenizer vocabulary. If control delimiters are composed of multi-token natural text sequences (such as the string `Observation:`), the model risks generating the delimiter text during reasoning, prematurely ending its turn or spoofing environmental inputs.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        ACB Execution Event Trace                        |
|  [Init Config] -> [User Query] -> [Thought + Tool Call] -> [Tool Return] |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                     |
                                     v
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                      Serialization & Hygiene Engine                     |
|  * Causal Sequence Sorting          * Control Token Escape Sanitation   |
|  * Delimiter Injection              * Whitespace & Payload Truncation   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                     |
                                     v
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                  Contiguous Training Sequence Buffer                    |
| <|sys|>...<|end|> <|user|>...<|end|> <|asst|><|th|>..<|call|>..<|end|>  |
| <|env|>...<|end|>                                                       |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

::: {#fig-sft-serialization-pipeline}
```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    subgraph ACB["Agent Control Block (ACB) Event Log"]

    S3 --> T3
```
The serialization pipeline transforming an asynchronous Agent Control Block (ACB) event log into a canonical tokenized sequence buffer with unambiguous role boundaries.
:::

### Delimiter Misalignment and Execution Spoofing

The precision of role delimiter insertion directly dictates the integrity of the learned policy. A common failure in naive serialization pipelines occurs when role delimiters are placed off by a single token index during buffer assembly. Consider a pipeline serializing multi-turn terminal interactions where the opening observation tag `<|start_tool_output|>` is accidentally assigned to the model generation sequence rather than the environment payload.

```
CORRECT DELIMITER ASSIGNMENT:
Assistant Generation:  `{"name": "read_file", "path": "main.py"}<|end_action|>`
Environment Injection: `<|start_tool_output|>\ndef process_batch():...<|end_tool_output|>`

OFF-BY-ONE DELIMITER LEAKAGE:
Assistant Generation:  `{"name": "read_file", "path": "main.py"}<|start_tool_output|>\ndef process_batch():`
Environment Injection: `...<|end_tool_output|>`
```

Under this off-by-one error, the autoregressive training objective forces the model to predict both its own action and the leading tokens of the simulated environment response. During subsequent inference, when the fine-tuned model emits the closing brace of its tool call, it does not yield control to the execution engine. Instead, it emits `<|start_tool_output|>` and hallucinates the file contents or database records. The runtime dispatcher never receives an RPC call; the model has learned an invalid closed-loop transition model that bypasses the real environment entirely.

### Causal Information Isolation

Every serialized trajectory must strictly preserve physical temporal causality. In an autoregressive model trained with a causal attention mask, the token representation at step $k$ conditions on all preceding tokens in the context window. Therefore, the prefix preceding decision step $k$ must contain exclusively the information that was physically present in the agent memory buffer at the instant the inference request was dispatched.

Temporal leakage occurs when serialization engines aggregate execution artifacts after trajectory completion and inject them retroactively into early positions in the context buffer. Examples include:

- Inserting post-hoc error diagnostic summaries into the initial system prompt.
- Rewriting tool schemas mid-stream based on versions retrieved at the end of the session.
- Injecting final trajectory task success flags into intermediate reasoning traces.

When an example contains temporal leakage, the policy is conditioned on future observations. The neural network learns spurious correlations, utilizing hidden future signals to choose actions rather than reasoning over intermediate observations. Once deployed, the future signal is absent, and policy performance degrades rapidly. Serialization routines must enforce causal monotonic timestamps across every event: for every step $k$ occurring at timestamp $T_k$, all tokens preceding step $k$ must have arrived at physical times $t < T_k$.

### Normalization of Non-Deterministic Observations

Environmental observations are inherently noisy, non-deterministic, and frequently unbound in size. Raw stdout streams contain ANSI terminal escape sequences, carriage returns (`\r`), dynamic process identifiers (PIDs), and non-deterministic clock times. If ingested raw into serialization pipelines, these volatile tokens consume significant context memory while offering zero invariant behavioral signal.

The serialization layer must apply strict normalization rules:

1. **ANSI and Control Code Stripping**: Terminal formatting sequences (colors, cursor repositioning) must be sanitized while preserving semantically meaningful indentation and line breaks.
2. **Schema Canonicalization**: Structured outputs from JSON-RPC calls must be normalized into a stable key-sorted serialization. Whitespace must follow an invariant indentation convention across all examples to prevent the model from allocating capacity to predicting arbitrary whitespace permutations.
3. **Budgeted Truncation**: When tool outputs exceed the context window budget, truncation must follow a deterministic retention policy. Naive head-truncation drops the initial command output or error code; naive tail-truncation cuts off final error messages or stack traces. The serialization contract must implement structural folding: retaining the initial invocation header and the final termination status while collapsing intermediate verbose rows into a deterministic token placeholder (such as `[... 842 lines truncated ...]`).

### Rationale Preservation and Structural Separation

High-performing agent policies rely on internal chain-of-thought traces to decompose subgoals before emitting action tokens. The serialization pipeline must preserve these intermediate deliberation traces without conflating cognitive reasoning with executable syntax.

Deliberation steps and tool execution calls must be serialized into separate structural sub-blocks inside the `Assistant` turn:

```xml
<|start_assistant|>
<|thought|>
The compilation failed due to a missing type annotation in worker.py line 42.
I must inspect worker.py around line 42 to verify the argument signature.
<|end_thought|>
<|call:read_file|>
{"filepath": "src/worker.py", "start_line": 35, "end_line": 50}
<|end_call|>
<|end_assistant|>
```

This structural separation is an architectural prerequisite for multi-task optimization. It allows the training runtime to distinguish between deliberative language modeling and strict syntax adherence.

Once an entire execution trajectory has been successfully serialized into a standardized, causally sound token buffer as illustrated in @fig-sft-serialization-pipeline, the training system faces an immediate optimization decision: across this thousands-of-tokens-long sequence, which specific subset of tokens should contribute to parameter gradient updates? As examined in @sec-vol3-sft-loss, computing cross-entropy loss indiscriminately across all tokens fundamentally corrupts the agent policy.

## Action-Targeted Loss Masking {#sec-vol3-sft-loss-masking}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Action-Targeted Loss Masking {#sec-vol3-sft-loss-masking}`
- **The Single Key Point:** Supervised loss must be strictly masked to compute cross-entropy over model-generated action and rationale tokens, setting loss over environment-returned observation tokens to zero.
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - A team fine-tunes a 7B parameter model on 10,000 tool-use trajectories without loss masking. When deployed, the model suffers a 45% drop in tool execution accuracy.     $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\theta) = -\sum_{t=1}^T m_t \cdot \log P_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})$$
    where the binary mask $m_t = 1$ if token $x_t$ was produced by the agent (action, tool call, rationale), and $m_t = 0$ if $x_t$ was produced by the system or environment (observations, prompts).
  - *Why Masking is Mandatory:* The model is not responsible for predicting external environment behavior; predicting compiler error messages or database responses wastes gradient capacity and induces hallucinated self-play.

- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Figure: Action-Targeted Loss Mask [insert link here: books/vol3/13_sft/images/svg/trajectory_loss_masking.svg] (Visualizing the binary mask $m_t$ overlaid across System, User, Action, and Observation tokens).

In a standard autoregressive language modeling objective, every token in a training sequence contributes uniformly to the optimization landscape. In an agentic execution pipeline, however, sequence buffers are fundamentally heterogeneous: they interleave immutable system instructions, user intents, internal agent rationales, structured tool calls, and high-volume external environment observations.

Consider an engineering team adapting a 7-billion-parameter base model across an archive of 10,000 multi-turn coding and tool-use trajectories. In a naive causal language modeling implementation where cross-entropy loss is computed over all tokens, the resulting checkpoint exhibits an immediate 45% degradation in tool execution accuracy relative to the base model upon deployment. Profiling the training logs reveals the root cause: 82% of the sequence tokens—and consequently 82% of the cumulative backward-pass gradient mass—originated from compiler outputs, git diffs, and JSON responses returned by external APIs. By penalizing the model for failing to predict external environment state, the optimization process spent four-fifths of its parameter capacity memorizing volatile runtime payloads rather than learning the operational policy.

### The Loss Masking Formalism

Supervised policy adaptation requires an explicit mathematical boundary between the agent policy and the external environment. Given a serialized trajectory represented as an ordered sequence of discrete tokens $x = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_T)$, the training objective applies a binary action mask $m_t \in \{0, 1\}$ at each token position:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\theta) = -\sum_{t=1}^T m_t \cdot \log P_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})$$

The indicator value $m_t$ is determined strictly by token provenance:

$$m_t = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x_t \in \mathcal{T}_{\text{agent}} \quad (\text{rationale, tool syntax, argument schemas}) \\ 0 & \text{if } x_t \in \mathcal{T}_{\text{env}} \quad (\text{system prompts, user inputs, environment observations}) \end{cases}$$

At the hardware execution layer, the forward pass processes the entire context $x_{1:T}$ through the transformer backbone to construct causal key-value representations across the full trajectory history. However, during loss computation, target labels corresponding to $m_t = 0$ are assigned to an ignore sentinel value (conventionally $-100$ in standard GPU cross-entropy kernels). This zeroes the upstream gradient vector:

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_t} = 0 \quad \text{for all } t \text{ where } m_t = 0$$

where $z_t$ represents the unnormalized logits at sequence step $t$. Parameter updates in the backward pass are computed exclusively from transitions initiated by the agent.

![Action-targeted loss masking across a multi-turn trajectory buffer. Cross-entropy loss is computed exclusively over agent-generated tokens (rationale and structured tool invocations), while system prompts, user instructions, and environment observation payloads are masked ($m_t = 0$), setting their gradient contributions to zero.](images/svg/trajectory_loss_masking.svg){#fig-trajectory-loss-masking}

### Decoupling Policy from Environment State

The requirement for loss masking originates from the architectural separation between the agent policy and the environment transition function. An agent policy is a mapping from observation histories to executable actions: $\pi_\theta(a \mid s)$. It is not an environmental emulator. The tokens contained within an observation block—such as non-deterministic process identifiers, network socket errors, memory heap addresses, or compiler stack traces—are generated by external operating systems and remote runtimes.

When a training harness forces an autoregressive network to compute cross-entropy over observation tokens, two severe failure modes manifest:

1. **Capacity Depletion**: The high entropy and Kolmogorov complexity of arbitrary terminal outputs and raw data streams consume valuable gradient bandwidth. The model allocates parameter capacity to modeling environment noise rather than stabilizing action syntax.
2. **Hallucinated Self-Play**: As demonstrated by Schick et al. (2023) in *Toolformer*, language models learn tool usage by recognizing the precise structural boundaries under which to dispatch an API call and yield execution. If observation tokens are unmasked during training, the model learns the joint distribution of both the command and its execution response. At inference time, upon emitting the terminating delimiter of an action, the model fails to yield control to the runtime. Instead, it autocompletes the predicted stdout payload internally, bypassing the physical RPC dispatcher entirely and operating in a disconnected, hallucinatory closed loop.

### Selective Masking: Rationale versus Action

Within the agent-generated token subset $\mathcal{T}_{\text{agent}}$, production architectures must navigate the trade-off between intermediate deliberation tokens (chain-of-thought rationales) and functional action tokens (tool names and structured argument schemas).

Two primary masking configurations exist in production systems:

- **Full Agent Supervision ($m_{\text{thought}} = 1, m_{\text{action}} = 1$)**: Both the natural language reasoning traces and the executable syntax receive gradient updates. This preserves the multi-step deductive pathways required to decompose ambiguous user requests into structured tool calls. However, because natural language reasoning frequently accounts for 70% to 90% of the agent turn, the gradient signal can become dominated by prose style and verbosity rather than syntactic precision.
- **Action-Only Supervision ($m_{\text{thought}} = 0, m_{\text{action}} = 1$)**: Deliberation tokens remain in the context buffer to condition causal attention, but backpropagation is restricted strictly to action delimiters, tool identifiers, and argument payloads. This concentrates parameter adaptation entirely on schema adherence and reduces catastrophic forgetting in core reasoning circuits. The primary operational risk is reasoning decoupling: because the deliberation tokens do not receive direct gradient feedback, the policy may generate rationales that contradict the simultaneously emitted tool parameters during zero-shot evaluation.

### The Token Denominator Problem

While binary masking isolates the optimization signal to valid decision boundaries, it introduces a severe numerical imbalance across training batches. In multi-turn workflows, individual trajectories exhibit radical variance in active token density: a sequence containing deep code analysis may yield thousands of active reasoning tokens, whereas a sequence containing an automated file search may yield only twenty action tokens wrapped around a 4,000-token directory listing.

If batch loss is normalized naively by total sequence length $T$, batches rich in observation data suffer vanishing gradients. Conversely, normalizing strictly by active token count $N_{\text{active}} = \sum m_t$ causes isolated action tokens to trigger volatile, destabilizing parameter updates. Furthermore, allocating fixed-length padded tensors for variable-density sequences severely underutilizes accelerator memory. As examined in @sec-vol3-sft-batching, scaling multi-turn policy adaptation requires specialized trajectory packing algorithms, dynamic sequence binning, and loss normalization strategies engineered to maintain stable gradient norms across heterogeneous execution lengths.

## Sequence Packing Isolation {#sec-vol3-sft-batching}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Sequence Packing Isolation {#sec-vol3-sft-batching}`
- **The Single Key Point:** Normalizing loss across heterogeneous trajectories dictates policy priorities; sequence packing requires document attention masking to prevent context cross-talk.
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - During distributed SFT, multiple short bash commands (50 tokens) and long file refactoring traces (8,000 tokens) are packed into a single 16,384-token sequence. Because standard causal attention was used without document boundary masks, the model in Trajectory 2 attends to file paths from Trajectory 1, hallucinating non-existent files during deployment.
- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**
  - *Normalization Dynamics: Per-Token vs. Per-Example:*
    - *Per-Token Normalization:* Divides total batch loss by the sum of active action tokens. Tends to over-weight long, multi-step trajectories at the expense of concise single-step decisions.
    - *Per-Example Normalization:* Computes mean loss per trajectory before averaging across the batch. Ensures equal gradient contribution across task types regardless of trace length.
  - *Sequence Packing with Block-Diagonal Attention:* Packing variable-length trajectories into fixed GPU buffer blocks to eliminate padding waste, using 2D block-diagonal attention masks to guarantee zero attention leakage across independent tasks.
  - *Truncation Hazards:* Why naive sequence truncation that cuts off terminal test results or compensating actions severely corrupts policy learning.
- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Diagram: Block-Diagonal Attention Mask for Packed Multi-Trajectory Training Sequences.
- **Causal Bridge to 13.4:** Even if loss masking and packing are perfectly implemented, why does an SFT model frequently fail when deployed in live interactive environments?
-->

In distributed supervised fine-tuning, multi-turn agent trajectories exhibit extreme variance in sequence length. An automated shell verification trace may consume 80 tokens, whereas a multi-file refactoring session encompassing compiler diagnostics and abstract syntax trees spans 12,000 tokens. Allocating fixed-length padded tensors sized to the maximum context window ($L_{\max} = 16,384$) produces severe hardware underutilization: if the mean trajectory length across an agent corpus is $\bar{T} = 2,048$ tokens, the operational matrix arithmetic achieves only $\bar{T} / L_{\max} = 12.5\%$ compute utilization, squandering 87.5% of accelerator FLOPs on masked padding tokens. To saturate tensor cores, modern training harnesses pack multiple variable-length trajectories into a single contiguous sequence buffer. However, naive concatenation without physical attention isolation introduces catastrophic cross-talk. If standard lower-triangular causal attention is evaluated across a packed buffer without sequence boundary enforcement, the attention projections of subsequent trajectories attend directly to the key-value states of preceding, unrelated tasks. When an agent fine-tuned under unisolated concatenation is deployed, an execution thread operating on a clean repository attends across its context boundaries to spurious file paths, network ports, or authentication tokens observed in previously packed traces.

### Normalization Dynamics: Per-Token versus Per-Example

Managing heterogeneous trajectories within packed batches requires resolving the normalization denominator of the empirical cross-entropy loss. Consider a training batch comprising $B$ packed trajectories $\{\tau_1, \tau_2, \dots, \tau_B\}$, where each trajectory $\tau_i$ contains $T_i$ total tokens and $N_i = \sum_{t=1}^{T_i} m^{(i)}_t$ active action tokens subjected to loss masking. Two distinct normalization paradigms dictate how the parameter update vector $\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}$ weights agent behaviors:

1. **Per-Token Normalization**: Loss is accumulated globally across all active tokens and divided by the aggregate active token count:
   $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{token}} = \frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^B N_i} \sum_{i=1}^B \sum_{t=1}^{T_i} m^{(i)}_t \cdot \ell(x^{(i)}_t, x^{(i)}_{<t})$$
   Under per-token weighting, long trajectories dominate the parameter update. A multi-turn refactoring trace generating $N_i = 4,000$ active reasoning tokens exerts one hundred times more influence on gradient direction than a single-turn terminal invocation where $N_j = 40$. Consequently, the policy over-indexes on verbose code modifications, while the gradient signal required to stabilize brittle, low-token operational primitives—such as emitting exact JSON delimiters or shell return codes—is diluted to numerical insignificance.

2. **Per-Example Normalization**: Cross-entropy is normalized locally within each trajectory before computing the unweighted mean across the batch:
   $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{example}} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B \left( \frac{1}{N_i} \sum_{t=1}^{T_i} m^{(i)}_t \cdot \ell(x^{(i)}_t, x^{(i)}_{<t}) \right)$$
   Per-example normalization guarantees that every operational decision boundary carries equal optimization priority regardless of context length. A concise bash invocation receives the same gradient contribution ($1/B$) as an expansive software rewrite. However, per-example weighting introduces high gradient variance when $N_i$ is small; a single mispredicted token in a sequence with $N_i = 2$ scales the gradient vector by $0.5 / B$, which can destabilize optimizer momentum buffers. Production training harnesses mitigate this by setting a floor on trajectory token denominators or applying square-root scaling ($\sqrt{N_i}$) to balance sequence importance against gradient stability.

### Sequence Packing and Block-Diagonal Attention

Eliminating padding overhead while preventing context leakage requires two synchronized mechanisms: greedy bin-packing and block-diagonal attention masking. Trajectories are assembled into fixed buffers of length $L_{\max}$ using first-fit decreasing bin-packing algorithms, ordering traces to minimize fragmentation at the sequence tail. Within the packed buffer, cross-trajectory attention must be strictly zeroed. Formally, for a packed buffer containing multiple concatenated trajectories, the attention affinity matrix between query position $j$ and key position $k$ is constrained by trajectory membership:

$$A_{j, k} = \begin{cases} \frac{q_j k_k^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} & \text{if } j \ge k \text{ and } \text{doc\_id}(j) = \text{doc\_id}(k) \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

![Block-diagonal causal attention mask for packed multi-trajectory training sequences. Independent trajectories ($\tau_1, \tau_2, \tau_3$) are packed into a single contiguous context window to eliminate padding waste. Off-diagonal attention blocks are masked to $-\infty$ (or skipped via variable-length kernel offsets), preventing causal cross-talk across disparate tasks while positional embeddings are reset at each trajectory boundary.](images/svg/packed_attention_mask.svg){#fig-packed-attention-mask}

Early packing implementations allocated explicit 2D boolean masks of dimension $L_{\max} \times L_{\max}$, consuming substantial memory bandwidth. Modern execution engines bypass dense mask allocation entirely by utilizing variable-length attention kernels, such as FlashAttention-2 varlen. The physical boundaries of each trajectory are passed to the accelerator SRAM tiling kernel as a 1D cumulative sequence offset array:

$$\mathbf{c} = [0, T_1, T_1 + T_2, \dots, \sum_{i=1}^B T_i]$$

The kernel constrains memory loads and online softmax normalizations strictly to row and column tiles within $[c_i, c_{i+1})$, enforcing hardware-level sequence isolation at zero memory overhead (@fig-packed-attention-mask).

Furthermore, sequence isolation requires resetting positional embeddings at document boundaries. If position indices increment monotonically across the packed sequence ($p_t = t \in [0, L_{\max}-1]$), trajectories placed at the tail of the buffer are evaluated under artificially elevated positional coordinates. In rotary position embedding (RoPE) implementations, this shifts query and key representations into high-frequency angular rotations reserved for long-context extrapolation, distorting the model's learned representation of local syntax. Runtimes must reset positional indices to zero at each boundary ($p^{(i)}_t = t - c_i$), ensuring that individual trajectories preserve identical positional geometry whether processed in isolation or packed alongside unrelated tasks.

### Truncation Hazards

When candidate trajectories exceed available bin capacities, training pipelines frequently apply naive sequence truncation, severing tokens that overflow $L_{\max}$. In agent policy training, arbitrary truncation introduces severe behavioral corruption:

- **Broken Action-Observation Loops**: Severing the context during an ongoing tool call forces the network to calculate gradients on unclosed schemas or partial argument payloads without observing the corresponding environment response.
- **Credit Assignment Inversion**: Consider an agent that executes an erroneous command (such as deleting an active configuration file), observes an error trace, and subsequently issues a compensating action (restoring from version control). If truncation severs the sequence immediately following the error observation, the backpropagation pass optimizes the policy to emit the destructive action without conditioning on the corrective sequence. The policy learns the failure mode as an acceptable terminal behavior.

To prevent policy corruption, production data loaders enforce atomic trajectory admission: trajectories exceeding context thresholds are either rejected, dynamically partitioned strictly at clean turn boundaries with re-initialized system prompts, or assigned to dedicated long-context training queues.

### The Limits of Open-Loop Cloning

Even when action loss masking is applied cleanly and block-diagonal packing prevents cross-trajectory attention leakage, supervised fine-tuning remains an open-loop cloning process. Training under teacher forcing assumes that the policy is evaluated exclusively along states visited by expert demonstrations. In live environments, however, any minor out-of-distribution observation or syntactic drift places the agent into novel states unrepresented in the supervised corpus. Because the model was never trained to recover from its own compounding errors, small inference mistakes trigger cascading operational failures—a structural limitation that demands interactive policy optimization and reinforcement learning.

<!-- SECTION_END: 13.3 -->

<!-- SECTION_START: 13.4 (#sec-vol3-sft-exposure-bias) -->
## Autoregressive Exposure Bias {#sec-vol3-sft-exposure-bias}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Autoregressive Exposure Bias {#sec-vol3-sft-exposure-bias}`
- **The Single Key Point:** Supervised policies trained exclusively on teacher-forced paths suffer catastrophic exposure bias; encountering an unfamiliar error state in live execution leads to compounding failure.
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - An agent trained via SFT on perfect Git workflows encounters an uncommitted merge conflict in production. Because the teacher-forced training corpus never contained merge conflict markers, the model enters an error-compounding spiral: it repeatedly runs `git status`, emits invalid flags, and eventually crashes the execution budget.
- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**
  - *The Mechanics of Exposure Bias:* During training (teacher forcing), the model predicts token $x_t$ conditioned on ground-truth history $x_{<t}^*$. During inference, it conditions on its own prior predictions $\hat{x}_{<t}$. A single minor error shifts the context outside the training distribution.
  - *Compounding Errors in Sequential Trajectories:* In an $N$-step trajectory, if the probability of staying on-distribution is $(1-\epsilon)$ per step, the probability of successful trajectory completion degrades exponentially:
    $$P(\text{success}) \le (1-\epsilon)^N \approx 1 - N\epsilon$$
  - *Mitigation via Dataset Aggregation (DAgger):*
    1. Roll out current student policy $\pi_\theta$ in the interactive environment.
    2. When the student makes a sub-optimal or erroneous choice, have an expert or verifier supply the correct recovery action.
    3. Aggregate recovery tuples into the training set and retrain.
  - *Controlled Fault Injection:* Deliberately injecting corrupt environment states during training data synthesis to force exposure to off-nominal conditions.
- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Trajectory Divergence Diagram: The Teacher-Forced Manifold vs. Autoregressive Drift and Recovery.
- **Seminal Literature:**
  - Stéphane Ross, Geoffrey Gordon, & J. Andrew Bagnell (2011, *A Reduction of Imitation Learning and Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning* / DAgger).
- **Causal Bridge to 13.5:** When adapting massive foundation models on long-context trajectories, how do we fit training into physical accelerator memory?
-->

The fundamental defect of supervised policy cloning stems from the discrepancy between the training state-transition operator and the deployment runtime. During supervised fine-tuning under teacher forcing, the loss function optimizes the likelihood of emitting token $x_t$ conditioned strictly on the ground-truth prefix $x_{<t}^*$:

$$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{t=1}^T \log \pi_\theta(x_t^* \mid x_{<t}^*)$$

At inference time, ground-truth tokens $x_{<t}^*$ do not exist. The generation runtime autoregressively appends the policy's own sampled tokens $\hat{x}_{<t} \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid \hat{x}_{<t-1})$ to the key-value (KV) cache. The moment the model emits a single out-of-distribution token—whether an unexpected JSON delimiter, a hallucinated command-line argument, or an invalid type cast—the prefix fed into subsequent attention operations shifts from the empirical distribution of demonstrations $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$ into unmodeled state space. Because open-loop cross-entropy training provides zero gradient feedback on states outside the expert demonstrations, the policy's conditional output distribution over recovery actions becomes undefined.

### Compounding Failures in Sequential Execution

In single-turn sequence-to-sequence tasks, exposure bias manifests as mild stylistic drift or degraded token perplexity. In agentic execution environments, where trajectories consist of $N$ discrete tool-invocation boundaries, exposure bias causes catastrophic compounding failure.

Consider an agent trained via supervised fine-tuning on clean Git maintenance workflows. The training corpus consists exclusively of successful executions: `git checkout -b`, `git add`, `git commit`, and `git push`. In production, the agent encounters an uncommitted rebase conflict containing standard conflict markers (`<<<<<<< HEAD`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`). Because the teacher-forced training distribution contained zero examples of raw conflict markers or failed rebase states, the model's attention heads disperse across the unfamiliar tokens rather than resolving the diff. The agent falls into an error-compounding spiral: it executes `git status`, receives the conflict output again, re-evaluates the unfamiliar context, issues an invalid flag such as `git commit --force-resolve`, and loops until it hits the runtime step limit ($T_{\max} = 30$) or exhausts its context window budget ($B_{\text{tokens}} = 128\text{k}$), resulting in zero trajectory goodput ($G = 0$).

![The trajectory divergence manifold in supervised agent training. Under standard teacher forcing, training updates optimize exclusively along the nominal expert trajectory (green manifold). During live autoregressive rollout, an unhandled environment fault or out-of-distribution action pushes the state off-manifold into unmodeled regions (red path), where standard SFT policies exhibit compounding divergence. Mitigations such as DAgger and synthetic fault injection incorporate corrective trajectories (blue path) that steer the policy back onto the nominal operational path.](images/svg/trajectory_exposure_bias.svg){#fig-trajectory-exposure-bias}

The physics of sequential error propagation explains this failure mode. Let each autonomous tool invocation have an independent probability $(1 - \epsilon)$ of staying within the nominal distribution, where $\epsilon$ represents the single-step error rate. Across an $N$-step operational pipeline, the probability of successful trajectory completion $P(\text{success})$ degrades exponentially:

$$P(\text{success}) \le (1 - \epsilon)^N \approx 1 - N\epsilon \quad (\text{for } N\epsilon \ll 1)$$

For a model with an apparently reliable single-step accuracy of $98\%$ ($\epsilon = 0.02$), a 20-step software refactoring workflow achieves a completion bound of $P(\text{success}) \le (0.98)^{20} \approx 0.668$. A 50-step deployment pipeline drops to $(0.98)^{50} \approx 0.364$. In real systems, the independent-error assumption is an optimistic upper bound; errors are serially correlated. Once an agent emits an invalid argument or receives an unhandled `stderr` returncode, the conditional probability of a subsequent failure approaches unity:

$$P(\text{error}_{t+1} \mid \text{error}_t) \gg \epsilon$$

Without explicit recovery training, a single off-manifold deviation induces an irreversible cascade (@fig-trajectory-exposure-bias).

### Closed-Loop Recovery via Dataset Aggregation

Mitigating exposure bias requires closing the loop between the model's empirical state visitation distribution and its optimization objective. The foundational formalization of this principle is Dataset Aggregation (DAgger), established by Stéphane Ross, Geoffrey Gordon, and J. Andrew Bagnell (2011). Rather than training exclusively on pre-collected static traces, DAgger aligns the training distribution with the student's induced policy distribution through iterative rollouts:

1. **Policy Rollout**: Execute the current policy checkpoint $\pi_\theta$ directly within an interactive execution sandbox.
2. **Off-Manifold Discovery**: Allow the policy to sample actions until it encounters an error, enters an unfamiliar observation state $\hat{s}_t$, or deviates from task criteria.
3. **Oracle Correction**: At state $\hat{s}_t$, invoke an expert policy (such as a frontier reasoning model or a verified deterministic oracle) to generate the optimal corrective action $a^*_{\text{recover}}$.
4. **Dataset Aggregation and Re-Tuning**: Append the newly visited off-manifold states and corresponding corrective actions $\{(\hat{s}_t, a^*_{\text{recover}})\}$ into the training buffer $\mathcal{D} \leftarrow \mathcal{D} \cup \mathcal{D}_{\text{recover}}$, and fine-tune $\pi_\theta$ over the combined distribution.

By iteratively conditioning the policy on its own induced errors during training, DAgger transforms open-loop imitation into a closed-loop controller. The optimization objective shifts from merely memorizing nominal paths to minimizing the distance between the student and expert across the entire reachable state space, bounding trajectory error growth linearly with $N$ rather than exponentially.

### Controlled Fault Injection

While interactive oracles provide robust recovery guarantees, continuous online rollouts against production environments can be prohibitively slow and expensive. Production training pipelines approximate closed-loop recovery via *controlled fault injection* during offline synthetic data generation.

Rather than synthesizing only successful traces, synthetic trace engines deliberately inject realistic operating system and network faults into intermediate observation steps:

- **Transient Network and Service Failures**: Injecting `HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout`, socket hang-ups, or rate-limit throttles (`429 Too Many Requests`) directly following API calls.
- **Filesystem and Permission Errors**: Simulating read-only filesystems, disk-space exhaustion (`ENOSPC`), or missing file descriptors following bash executions.
- **Syntax and Environment Corruption**: Providing corrupted dependency lockfiles, merge conflict delimiters, or partially truncated terminal outputs.

When a synthetic fault is injected, the trace generator forces the expert model to emit diagnostic and remediation actions—such as parsing the `stderr` message, running filesystem checks, applying exponential backoff, or reverting uncommitted changes via version control. Exposing the network's attention layers to corrupted observation tokens during teacher-forced training ensures that when an inference-time divergence occurs, the model attends to valid recovery pathways rather than entering an unconstrained failure loop.

### Memory Bottlenecks in Long-Context Adaptation

Expanding training corpora to include multi-turn recovery sequences, fault-injection traces, and expanded tool schemas inflates the sequence lengths required for policy optimization. Processing 32,768-token interaction traces under full-parameter backpropagation imposes extreme physical demands on accelerator hardware. Storing dense intermediate activations, rotary embeddings, and optimizer states for modern multi-billion-parameter foundation models rapidly exceeds the physical High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) capacity of individual accelerators (such as 80 GB H100 SXM5 nodes). To execute supervised adaptation on realistic agent traces without prohibitive compute clusters, training architectures must move beyond naive full-parameter updates toward parameter-efficient adaptation and memory-optimized execution kernels.

<!-- SECTION_END: 13.4 -->

<!-- SECTION_START: 13.5 (#sec-vol3-sft-peft) -->
## Parameter-Efficient Memory Bounds {#sec-vol3-sft-peft}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Parameter-Efficient Memory Bounds {#sec-vol3-sft-peft}`
- **The Single Key Point:** Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) dramatically reduces optimizer and gradient accelerator memory, enabling multi-tenant adapter swapping, but leaves the activation memory bottleneck during long-context backpropagation unchanged.
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - An ML infrastructure team attempts full fine-tuning of a 70B parameter model on 32k-token trajectories across 8x 80GB H100 GPUs. The job instantly crashes with an Out-of-Memory (OOM) error during the backward pass. Switching to LoRA ($r=16$) reduces optimizer memory from 1.12 TB to 28 GB, but the job *still* crashes during attention backprop until gradient checkpointing and FlashAttention-2 are enabled.
- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**
  - *Accelerator Memory Accounting in Trajectory Training:*
    $$M_{\text{total}} = M_{\text{weights}} + M_{\text{gradients}} + M_{\text{optimizer}} + M_{\text{activations}}(B, T, L, H)$$
    - *Full SFT (AdamW):* Requires 16 bytes per parameter (2 bytes weights, 2 bytes gradients, 12 bytes optimizer state). A 70B model requires 1.12 TB VRAM just for static state.
    - *LoRA Updates:* Freezes base weights $W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ and injects trainable low-rank matrices $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}, A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$ with $r \ll \min(d, k)$. Static memory drops by >90%.
  - *The Activation Memory Dominance:* For long-horizon agent trajectories ($T = 32\text{k}$ to $64\text{k}$ tokens), activation memory scales quadratically or linearly with sequence length:
    $$M_{\text{act}} \propto B \cdot L \cdot T \cdot d_{\text{model}}$$
    LoRA does *not* reduce activation memory. Memory savings must come from Selective Activation Checkpointing.
  - *Serving Implications: Dynamic Adapter Swapping:* LoRA enables serving dozens of specialized task policies (e.g. SQL specialist, Git specialist) on a single shared base model instance via dynamic LoRA kernel swapping.
- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Table: Accelerator Memory Breakdown (Full SFT vs. LoRA $r=16$ vs. QLoRA 4-bit) across 7B, 13B, and 70B model sizes.
- **Seminal Literature:**
  - Edward J. Hu et al. (2021, *LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models*).
- **Causal Bridge to 13.6:** How do we ensure that an adapted policy generalizes to new tool schemas rather than memorizing fixed API formats?
-->

Fine-tuning large language models on multi-turn agent trajectories introduces an asymmetric hardware bottleneck. While sequence lengths in standard natural language tasks rarely exceed $2,048$ to $4,096$ tokens, an agent trace containing environment observations, tool documentation, compiler outputs, and multi-turn error recovery loops easily spans $32,768$ to $65,536$ tokens.

Consider an infrastructure cluster attempting full-parameter supervised fine-tuning of a 70-billion-parameter dense model across eight 80 GB NVIDIA H100 GPUs connected via NVLink. The dataset consists of 32k-token environment traces. Upon launching the training job, the runtime immediately terminates with an Out-of-Memory (OOM) fault during the initial backward pass. Attempting to resolve the failure, the engineering team switches from full fine-tuning to Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA, $r=16$), successfully reducing optimizer memory from $1.12\text{ TB}$ to under $28\text{ GB}$. Yet, upon restarting, the job crashes at the exact same execution step with an identical OOM allocation failure.

Resolving this failure requires auditing the physical memory allocation of transformer backpropagation across sequence length, model dimensions, and optimization state.

### Accelerator Memory Accounting in Trajectory Training

The physical High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) demanded by an accelerator during training partitions into static allocations and dynamic runtime buffers:

$$M_{\text{total}} = M_{\text{weights}} + M_{\text{gradients}} + M_{\text{optimizer}} + M_{\text{activations}}(B, T, L, d_{\text{model}})$$

where $B$ is the micro-batch size per device, $T$ is the sequence length in tokens, $L$ is the number of transformer layers, and $d_{\text{model}}$ is the hidden state dimension.

Under standard 16-bit mixed-precision training (BF16 or FP16) using the AdamW optimizer, static state requirements scale strictly with the parameter count $N$:

1. **Model Weights ($M_{\text{weights}}$):** Storing parameters in 16-bit floating point requires $2N$ bytes.
2. **Gradients ($M_{\text{gradients}}$):** Storing backward pass gradients in 16-bit precision requires $2N$ bytes.
3. **Optimizer States ($M_{\text{optimizer}}$):** AdamW maintains three values per parameter in 32-bit floating point to ensure numerical stability: a master copy of the weights ($4N$ bytes), the first momentum buffer ($4N$ bytes), and the second raw variance buffer ($4N$ bytes), totaling $12N$ bytes.

Static memory totals $16N$ bytes. For a 70-billion-parameter foundation model ($N = 70 \times 10^9$), static state consumes:

$$M_{\text{static}} = 16 \times 70 \times 10^9 \text{ bytes} \approx 1.12\text{ TB}$$

Across an 8-GPU node of 80 GB accelerators ($640\text{ GB}$ total HBM), static state alone exceeds total physical capacity by $175\%$, before allocating a single byte for trajectory activations.

```
Full SFT (16-bit weights, AdamW): 16 bytes / parameter
+-------------------+-------------------+---------------------------------------+
| Weights (2B)      | Gradients (2B)    | Optimizer States (FP32 Master,        |
|                   |                   | Momentum, Variance: 12B)              |
+-------------------+-------------------+---------------------------------------+

LoRA (Frozen base W_0, trainable A & B with rank r << d):
+-------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------+
| Frozen Base (2B)  | Trainable Adapter (Weights + Grads + AdamW: ~0.04B)       |
+-------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------+

QLoRA (4-bit NF4 base W_0, double quantization, 16-bit LoRA adapter):
+---------+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Base    | Trainable Adapter Overhead                                          |
| (0.5B)  |                                                                     |
+---------+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

Low-Rank Adaptation (Edward J. Hu et al., 2021) eliminates this static footprint by freezing the pretrained weight matrix $W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ and injecting trainable rank-decomposition matrices:

$$W = W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A$$

where $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$, the rank satisfies $r \ll \min(d, k)$, and $\alpha$ is a constant scaling hyperparameter. Because $W_0$ remains static, it requires no gradient storage ($0$ bytes) and no optimizer states ($0$ bytes). Gradients and AdamW tracking apply exclusively to $A$ and $B$. When applying LoRA across all linear projection layers with rank $r=16$, trainable parameters typically comprise less than $0.2\%$ of the original parameter count, compressing static optimizer state from hundreds of gigabytes to mere hundreds of megabytes (@tbl-peft-memory-footprint).

| Model Size               | Full SFT Weights | Full SFT Static Total | LoRA ($r=16$) Static Total | QLoRA (4-bit) Static Total |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------|:----------------------|:---------------------------|:---------------------------|
| **7B** ($d=4096, L=32$)  | $14\text{ GB}$   | $112\text{ GB}$       | $14.3\text{ GB}$           | $4.1\text{ GB}$            |
| **13B** ($d=5120, L=40$) | $26\text{ GB}$   | $208\text{ GB}$       | $26.5\text{ GB}$           | $7.4\text{ GB}$            |
| **70B** ($d=8192, L=80$) | $140\text{ GB}$  | $1,120\text{ GB}$     | $142.8\text{ GB}$          | $38.5\text{ GB}$           |

: Accelerator Static Memory Footprint Across Model Scales and Adaptation Schemes. Full SFT assumes 16-bit mixed-precision with FP32 AdamW states ($16\text{ bytes/param}$). LoRA ($r=16$) assumes 16-bit base weights with adapter projections applied to all attention and feed-forward linear layers. QLoRA assumes NormalFloat4 (NF4) base weight quantization with 16-bit adapter states. {#tbl-peft-memory-footprint}

### The Activation Memory Bottleneck in Long-Horizon Trajectories

The recurrence of the OOM crash under LoRA highlights a fundamental architectural invariant: *parameter-efficient adaptation reduces static parameter and optimizer memory, but leaves activation memory completely uncompressed.*

During the forward pass of backpropagation, intermediate tensor activations at each layer must be preserved in HBM to compute gradients with respect to $A$ and $B$ during the backward pass. For a sequence length $T$, activation memory scales linearly with depth and sequence length:

$$M_{\text{act}} \propto B \cdot L \cdot T \cdot d_{\text{model}}$$

Without memory-efficient attention kernels, the attention logits construct an intermediate tensor of dimension $B \times H \times T \times T$, exhibiting quadratic scaling $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$. At $T = 32,768$ and 64 attention heads, materializing the raw attention matrix across 80 layers requires over $100\text{ GB}$ per sequence—exceeding device HBM on a single forward pass.

FlashAttention-2 eliminates the quadratic materialization of the $T \times T$ attention matrix by tiling computation within the streaming multiprocessor's local Static RAM (SRAM), bounding dynamic attention memory to $\mathcal{O}(T)$. However, intermediate linear layer activations (such as SwiGLU projection buffers and layer normalization inputs) remain stored in HBM.

To prevent activation OOMs on 32k-token trajectories, training pipelines must pair LoRA with *Selective Activation Checkpointing* (gradient checkpointing). Rather than preserving all intermediate layer activations throughout the entire forward pass, the runtime evicts the forward activations of selected transformer blocks from HBM, retaining only the layer boundary inputs. During the backward pass, the discarded activations are recomputed on-the-fly from the checkpointed boundary tensors. This trades a deterministic computational penalty (approximately $33\%$ additional floating-point operations) to reduce activation memory scaling from $\mathcal{O}(L \cdot T)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{L} \cdot T)$ or $\mathcal{O}(T)$ per layer.

### Serving Implications: Dynamic Multi-Tenant Adapter Swapping

Beyond training feasibility, the parameter efficiency of low-rank matrices transforms the deployment physics of production agent systems. In an enterprise operational workflow, a generalist agent must orchestrate diverse sub-domains: generating schema-compliant SQL queries, emitting valid Git branch operations, and generating Python diagnostic scripts.

Serving separate fine-tuned 70B parameter models for each sub-domain would require duplicating base weights across independent GPU clusters, incurring severe hardware costs and low resource utilization. Because LoRA decomposes adaptation into low-rank deltas, inference servers retain a single frozen copy of the base model weights $W_0$ in accelerator HBM. Specialized task policies exist as lightweight weight tensors ($A_k, B_k$), each consuming tens of megabytes on host storage.

When routing agent requests through multi-tenant serving runtimes (such as S-LoRA or Punica), the server executes batched matrix multiplication where the shared base transformation is computed once, and per-token adapter matrices are dynamically gathered and applied in high-speed SRAM caches:

$$y = x W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r} x A_k B_k$$

A single inference node can concurrently serve hundreds of specialized agent capabilities, swapping operational policies on a per-request basis without context reloading or base-model cold-start latency.

While parameter-efficient adaptation resolves accelerator memory bounds and facilitates dynamic dispatch, compressing policy updates into low-rank matrices introduces a critical operational challenge: policy overfitting. If the low-rank update memorizes specific environment tokens rather than underlying control logic, the agent fails when confronted with unseen tool interfaces. We must therefore examine how to structure supervised adaptation so that compiled policies generalize robustly to novel APIs and shifting operational schemas.

<!-- SECTION_END: 13.5 -->

<!-- SECTION_START: 13.6 (#sec-vol3-sft-schemas) -->
## Dynamic Schema Regularization {#sec-vol3-sft-schemas}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Dynamic Schema Regularization {#sec-vol3-sft-schemas}`
- **The Single Key Point:** Supervised fine-tuning risks memorizing fixed tool parameter formats; robust policy adaptation requires schema perturbation, parameter shuffling, and negative schema injection during training.
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - A coding agent fine-tuned on AWS CLI tools flawlessly executes cloud deployment scripts. However, when the cloud provider updates its CLI syntax from `--cluster-name` to `--cluster-id`, the agent completely ignores the new JSON schema provided in context and stubbornly emits the deprecated parameter, failing every invocation.
- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**
  - *The Mechanism of Schema Memorization:* When a model is fine-tuned repeatedly on fixed tool definitions, the attention weights between the task prompt and the tool definition attenuate; the model memorizes parameter names directly into feed-forward network weights.
  - *Schema Regularization Techniques:*
    1. *Dynamic Schema Permutation:* Shuffling the order of parameter keys in tool definitions across training examples.
    2. *Synonym & Identifier Perturbation:* Programmatically renaming tools and arguments (e.g. `read_file` $\rightarrow$ `fetch_document`) to force the policy to condition on the supplied schema.
    3. *Distractor Tool Injection:* Adding irrelevant tool definitions into the context during training to train the model to discriminate between candidate tools.
  - *Evaluating Out-of-Distribution Tool Generalization:* Testing adapted models against novel, unseen tool schemas at inference time.
- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Diagram: Schema Memorization vs. Context-Conditioned Tool Dispatch (Attention heatmaps showing reliance on weights vs. prompt schema).
- **Causal Bridge to 13.7:** How do we assemble a rigorous evaluation harness to prove that an adapted policy improves complete agent task performance?
-->

When an agent policy undergoes supervised fine-tuning on fixed environment interfaces, the optimization process frequently introduces an operational failure mode: the model memorizes static parameter tokens instead of learning dynamic, in-context schema binding. Consider a software engineering agent fine-tuned on cloud infrastructure CLI commands. During training, the tool schema specifies an orchestration command with a `--cluster-name` argument. If the cloud provider updates its CLI syntax to require `--cluster-id`, an unregularized adapted model will stubbornly emit `--cluster-name`, even when the prompt context explicitly supplies the new schema. The runtime execution environment rejects the invocation with an invalid argument error (`400 Bad Request: Unknown parameter`), halting execution goodput. The model treats tool invocation as the replay of static token sequences rather than a dynamic translation of user intent into the supplied interface specification.

### The Mechanics of Schema Memorization

This failure mode stems from how backpropagation allocates capacity across transformer layers during supervised fine-tuning. Autoregressive training optimizes the cross-entropy objective:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}} = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P(x_t \mid x_{<t}; \theta)$$

When training datasets pair a specific operational intent with identical tool and parameter names across thousands of trajectory steps, the mapping becomes deterministic. The optimization trajectory minimizes cross-entropy by encoding these invariant token sequences directly into the weight matrices of the feed-forward network (FFN) layers, which act as key-value associative memories.

As parameter weights memorize token identities, the multi-head attention circuits that route information from the prompt context to the generation positions undergo functional attenuation. For a query vector $q_i$ at generation step $i$ and key vector $k_j$ at context position $j$, the normalized attention weight is:

$$\alpha_{i,j} = \frac{\exp\left(\frac{q_i k_j^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)}{\sum_{m=1}^{N} \exp\left(\frac{q_i k_m^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)}$$

When argument strings are stored directly in FFN projections, the gradient signal no longer reinforces attention heads that align the output token $x_i$ with the corresponding schema definition tokens in the context window. Consequently, the cumulative attention mass directed at the schema token set $\mathcal{S}$, defined as $\sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} \alpha_{i,j}$, decays toward zero (@fig-schema-attention). The model degenerates into an open-loop generator governed by static weight priors, rendering it brittle to runtime interface mutations.

::: {#fig-schema-attention}
```
UNREGULARIZED MODEL (SCHEMA MEMORIZATION)
Context:   [System] ... [Schema: --cluster-id] ... [Task] ... [Emit: "--cluster-name"]
Attention:   0.02              0.03                  0.41                 0.54
           └───────────────────┴─────────────────────┴────────────────────┘
           Schema ignored; FFN weights emit memorized parameter from prior training

REGULARIZED MODEL (CONTEXT-CONDITIONED BINDING)
Context:   [System] ... [Schema: --cluster-id] ... [Task] ... [Emit: "--cluster-id"]
Attention:   0.01              0.81                  0.12                 0.06
           └───────────────────┴─────────────────────┴────────────────────┘
           High cross-attention to schema; parameter bound dynamically from prompt
```
Attention allocation during tool parameter generation. In an unregularized model, cross-attention to the in-context schema tokens attenuates, causing feed-forward network weights to emit memorized parameter keys. Dynamic schema regularization maintains high attention mass on context schema tokens, ensuring correct argument dispatch when interfaces change.
:::

### Schema Regularization Techniques

Preventing the optimizer from bypassing prompt context requires eliminating static token correlations during training data compilation. Three complementary techniques enforce context-conditioned schema resolution:

1. **Dynamic Schema Permutation:** In serializations such as JSON or YAML, key-value pairs are mathematically unordered, yet tokenizers serialize them into rigid sequential positions. If parameter key $A$ systematically precedes key $B$, positional embeddings reinforce an artificial sequential dependency. Dynamic schema permutation randomizes both the sequence of parameter definitions in the system prompt and the key ordering in the emitted invocation payload across training samples. This breaks positional heuristics, forcing attention heads to resolve argument dependencies based on semantic identity rather than relative token offsets.
2. **Identifier and Synonym Perturbation:** When tool definitions use common identifiers (such as `read_file` or `path`), pretrained representations and fine-tuning updates reinforce direct lexical shortcuts. Identifier perturbation programmatically alters names and keys at compilation time. For instance, `read_file(path, offset)` is mapped to synthetic variants such as `fetch_document(target_uri, byte_start)` or randomized identifiers such as `tool_842(arg_x, arg_y)`. Because synthetic identifiers carry no pretrained semantic weight, the model cannot rely on parameter memory to predict argument names; it must route attention directly to the supplied schema tokens to satisfy the loss function.
3. **Distractor Tool Injection:** Exposing the model solely to the minimal tool definitions required for a given trajectory creates an artificial inductive bias: the model learns that any tool present in the prompt must be invoked. In production runtimes, an agent must query registries containing dozens of heterogeneous tools. Distractor tool injection appends irrelevant tool schemas—such as administrative scripts, diagnostic monitors, or conflicting interface versions—into the training context. The training loss penalizes erroneous invocations, training the policy network to discriminate between candidate schemas and condition invocation choices strictly on alignment between user intent and schema definitions.

### Evaluating Out-of-Distribution Tool Generalization

Evaluating adapted policies exclusively against in-distribution validation splits creates a false sense of reliability: models that have memorized static schemas achieve near-zero validation loss while failing completely when interfaces evolve. Rigorous evaluation requires an out-of-distribution (OOD) validation suite structured around three core metrics:

1. **Schema Conformance Under Mutation:** The evaluation harness mutates the schemas of familiar tools by altering parameter names (such as converting `snake_case` keys to `camelCase` or substituting synonyms). Schema Conformance measures the proportion of tool invocations whose emitted keys strictly match the modified context schema rather than the training set defaults.
2. **Parameter Binding Accuracy:** To evaluate whether the model has acquired generalized interface binding rather than task-specific scripts, the policy is evaluated on held-out, completely synthetic APIs. Parameter Binding Accuracy measures the fraction of emitted tool calls that satisfy all interface constraints:

$$A_{\text{bind}} = \frac{N_{\text{valid}}}{N_{\text{total}}}$$

where $N_{\text{valid}}$ represents the count of generated tool calls containing valid argument names, expected types, and required structural keys as defined by the unseen schema, and $N_{\text{total}}$ is the total invocation count.

3. **Distractor Rejection Ratio:** In environments populated with high-density tool registries, this metric measures the policy's capacity to maintain selective invocation accuracy without executing irrelevant tools or generating hallucinated arguments.

Achieving high parameter binding accuracy and schema conformance provides the foundation for reliable tool execution, but syntactically valid invocations do not guarantee task completion. An agent may emit schema-perfect JSON payloads while pursuing fundamentally incorrect operational strategies, repeating failed actions, or compounding errors across multi-step execution graphs. To evaluate whether fine-tuning produces an effective end-to-end policy, we must construct evaluation harnesses that benchmark holistic trajectory goodput and long-horizon task completion, as developed in @sec-vol3-sft-eval.

<!-- SECTION_END: 13.6 -->

<!-- SECTION_START: 13.7 (#sec-vol3-sft-evaluation) -->
## Adapted Policy Benchmarking {#sec-vol3-sft-evaluation}

The optimization objective of supervised fine-tuning minimizes token-level cross-entropy loss under teacher forcing, yet this objective diverges sharply from closed-loop task execution. In a supervised training batch, the loss function evaluates conditional probability distributions over next tokens given ground-truth prior prefixes ($P(y_t \mid y_{<t}^*)$). At inference time, however, an autonomous agent executes as a stateful, closed-loop dynamical system where each generated token determines subsequent environment observations ($P(\hat{y}_t \mid \hat{y}_{<t})$). Compounding execution errors create a severe distribution shift between offline training loss and online trajectory performance.

Consider an empirical comparison between two checkpoints during policy adaptation: Checkpoint A (saved after epoch 1) and Checkpoint B (saved after epoch 5). Checkpoint B demonstrates a 25% lower cross-entropy validation loss on held-out trajectories than Checkpoint A. Yet, when deployed against the SWE-bench software engineering benchmark, Checkpoint B resolves 30% fewer issues than Checkpoint A. Inspection of the trajectory telemetry reveals why: Checkpoint B overfitted to specific stylistic and reasoning tokens present in the training set. During open-ended execution, it enters repetitive reasoning loops, emitting verbose diagnostic reflections until it exhausts the hard context window limit ($K_{\text{tokens}} > K_{\text{max}}$) without dispatching the required file-system modifications. Lower validation perplexity simply reflects higher statistical confidence in local token continuations; it does not measure goal convergence, error recovery, or adherence to global execution budgets.

### The Multi-Dimensional Evaluation Matrix

Benchmarking adapted policies requires replacing scalar loss metrics with an evaluation matrix spanning four orthogonal systems axes:

1. **State-Verified Task Completion ($R_{\text{task}}$):** Task success cannot rely on model self-reporting or linguistic plausibility. It must be computed via automated, external assertions on the target environment state. In software agents, this is binary verification via hermetic test suites (for example, whether the altered codebase passes existing unit tests plus hidden reproduction tests). In database or administrative agents, verification requires checking persistent state invariants against a formal schema post-execution.
2. **Syntactic and Semantic Tool Validity ($V_{\text{syntax}}$):** This metric measures the proportion of emitted tool invocations that parse cleanly into target schemas without runtime exceptions:
   $$V_{\text{syntax}} = \frac{N_{\text{valid\_calls}}}{N_{\text{total\_calls}}}$$
   Syntactic validity requires strictly formed serialization (such as valid JSON), presence of all non-optional arguments, and adherence to declared primitive types. Semantic validity additionally verifies that referenced entities—such as file paths, database identifiers, or process handles—exist within the active environment runtime.

3. **Trajectory Efficiency and Systems Goodput:** An agent policy that solves a task in 50 tool iterations while consuming 128,000 tokens is vastly inferior from a systems perspective to a policy that solves the same task in 4 iterations using 4,000 tokens. Execution efficiency is quantified by decomposed trajectory wall-clock latency:
   $$T_{\text{task}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( T_{\text{model}, i} + T_{\text{tool}, i} + T_{\text{runtime}, i} \right)$$
   where $T_{\text{model}}$ is generation latency (governed by prefill Time to First Token and inter-token decode latency), $T_{\text{tool}}$ is the execution latency of the tool subsystem, and $T_{\text{runtime}}$ represents middleware overhead (sandboxing, schema validation, and context serialization). System efficiency is summarized through Trajectory Goodput ($G$):
   $$G = \frac{\sum T_{\text{success}}}{\sum T_{\text{all}}}$$
   representing the fraction of total compute time dedicated to trajectories that successfully achieve their terminal objective.

4. **Regression on General Capabilities:** Narrow adaptation frequently degrades pretrained parameter circuits responsible for logical deduction, mathematical reasoning, and instruction following. A comprehensive evaluation harness must run adapted checkpoints through standard anchor suites (such as MMLU for factual reasoning, GSM8K for multi-step arithmetic, and HumanEval for base code synthesis) to compute an explicit capability degradation delta ($\Delta_{\text{cap}} = M_{\text{adapted}} - M_{\text{base}}$).

### Controlled Benchmarking Protocols

Evaluating an adapted agent policy requires an instrumentation harness that guarantees determinism and environment isolation. If the test harness invokes live APIs, variable network latency, fluctuating backend state, and non-deterministic rate limits corrupt latency and success metrics.

The evaluation harness must execute inside containerized microVM sandboxes instantiated from pinned base filesystem images. External tools—such as search engines, payment gateways, or web browsers—must run against recorded mock servers with deterministic response latencies. Randomness must be controlled by setting generation temperature to zero or pinning pseudo-random generator seeds across runs. Finally, every benchmark run must enforce strict systems invariants: maximum step count ($N \le N_{\text{max}}$), wall-clock execution timeouts ($T \le T_{\text{max}}$), and token budgets ($K \le K_{\text{max}}$). When a policy exceeds any budget envelope, the harness terminates execution and marks the trajectory as failed, preventing runaways from skewing fleet utilization statistics.

When an adapted model is validated through this matrix, engineering teams often discover that fine-tuning breaks down in subtle, counterintuitive ways across memory, serialization, and boundary conditions. We analyze these recurring failure modes and their mitigations in @sec-vol3-sft-fallacies.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-ch13-fallacies}

<!-- FALLACIES_SPEC:

- **Fallacy 1:** *Minimizing cross-entropy loss across all trajectory tokens optimizes agent behavior.*
  - Refutation: Unmasked loss forces the model to memorize external tool observations and environment outputs; loss must be strictly masked to target model-generated actions and rationale.
- **Pitfall 1:** *Assuming LoRA eliminates all memory constraints for long-context trajectories.*
  - Refutation: LoRA reduces weight, gradient, and optimizer memory, but activation memory during self-attention backpropagation scales linearly or quadratically with sequence length; long trajectories still require activation checkpointing.
- **Fallacy 2:** *A model fine-tuned on existing tool schemas will automatically generalize to updated schemas.*

- **Pitfall 2:** *Using sequence packing without 2D attention boundary masks.*

-->

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Minimizing cross-entropy loss across all trajectory tokens optimizes agent behavior.*

When computing autoregressive cross-entropy loss across an entire multi-turn trajectory, gradient descent optimizes the joint distribution over both agent outputs (internal reasoning and tool invocations) and environment outputs (system prompts, user instructions, and tool return values). Environment observations originate from non-stationary, non-differentiable external processes, such as database query dumps, API JSON responses, and operating system logs. Backpropagating through unmasked observation tokens forces model weights to expend representational capacity on predicting arbitrary external state transitions, entropy-rich runtime payloads, and stochastic error strings. This dynamic causes severe context poisoning and sample inefficiency: instead of learning the conditional policy distribution $\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)$, the model memorizes transient observation artifacts. At deployment, when novel observation payloads deviate slightly from training distributions, the overfitted token-level transition prior triggers catastrophic distribution shift, producing malformed tool calls or hallucinatory tool executions. Robust policy compilation requires strict loss masking over all input and environment sequences, setting label indices to $-100$ in standard tensor frameworks so that gradients backpropagate solely through tokens generated by the agent policy itself.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Assuming LoRA eliminates all memory constraints for long-context trajectories.*

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduces the parameter footprint of fine-tuning by freezing pretrained weights $W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ and learning rank decomposition matrices $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ with $r \ll \min(d, k)$. While this architecture drastically curtails static weight memory, gradient tensors, and Adam optimizer state allocations from sixteen bytes per parameter down to the low-rank adapter parameters, it leaves intermediate activation memory fundamentally untouched. During the backward pass of self-attention across multi-turn agent rollouts spanning thirty-two thousand or sixty-four thousand tokens, intermediate activations scale quadratically $\mathcal{O}(L^2)$ with un-fused attention or linearly $\mathcal{O}(L \cdot d)$ with memory-efficient attention engines such as FlashAttention. Every layer must retain query, key, value projections, attention dropout masks, and pre-activation states for the chain rule, which rapidly exhausts the High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) capacity of accelerator nodes. Engineers who fail to account for dynamic activation scaling encounter out-of-memory kernel panics during long-horizon rollouts despite running minimal adapter ranks. Mitigating this memory wall requires combining LoRA with activation checkpointing (recomputation during the backward pass), sequence parallelism across tensor devices, or selective activation offloading across the host interconnect.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *A model fine-tuned on existing tool schemas will automatically generalize to updated schemas.*

Fine-tuning an agent policy against a static corpus of tool documentation and API signatures compiles procedural semantics directly into feed-forward network weights. When the training dataset presents invariant interface definitions—such as static parameter names, rigid argument ordering, and fixed type constraints—gradient updates cause the model to bypass dynamic in-context parsing. The network establishes direct associative shortcuts between semantic intents and hardcoded token sequences of the schema. Consequently, when production environments deploy versioned API updates—such as renaming a parameter from `query` to `search_term`, deprecating a flag, or reordering structural fields—the policy exhibits severe functional regression. Model weights overrule the updated system prompt or dynamic schema block, emitting deprecated arguments and failing validation barriers. Overcoming this failure mode demands schema perturbation during supervised adaptation: training routines must systematically shuffle parameter ordering, inject synonymous key variations, alter JSON formatting schemas, and randomly supply synthetic schemas. Only by forcing the attention mechanism to attend dynamically to runtime interface specifications, rather than relying on internalized parameter projections, can compiled policies remain resilient to evolutionary changes in production tool contracts.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Using sequence packing without 2D attention boundary masks.*

Sequence packing concatenates multiple short agent trajectories into a single maximum-length context buffer (such as eight thousand or sixteen thousand tokens) to eliminate padding overhead and maximize hardware arithmetic intensity on accelerator systolic arrays. However, if the underlying transformer implementation relies on a standard causal triangular mask across the entire packed sequence, tokens from subsequent trajectories attend causally to trailing tokens of preceding, entirely unrelated trajectories. This structural oversight introduces catastrophic cross-trajectory attention contamination. The model experiences context poisoning during training, learning invalid cross-task causal dependencies and treating stale observations from prior execution graphs as valid historical priors. In production, this causes the compiled policy to hallucinate parameters, variables, and error states belonging to unrelated tasks or users. Preserving complete mathematical isolation across packed sequences requires constructing a block-diagonal 2D attention mask or resetting cumulative positional encodings at trajectory boundaries. Hardware-optimized attention kernels (such as FlashAttention with variable-length sequence metadata) must receive explicit cumulative sequence length arrays (`cu_seqlens`) to prevent attention score computation across episode boundaries, ensuring that computational packing efficiency does not degrade policy execution integrity.

:::

<!-- FALLACIES_END -->

## Summary {#sec-vol3-ch13-summary}
