Supervised policy adaptation functions as an offline compilation stage that translates ephemeral runtime demonstrations, schema specifications, and multi-turn interaction histories directly into the parametric substrate of a foundation model. By internalizing tool-calling protocols, interface grammars, and domain-specific decision boundaries into model weights, adaptation eliminates the latency, cost, and context-window degradation incurred by massive few-shot demonstration prompts while preserving general-purpose reasoning capabilities. However, treating multi-turn agent trajectories as standard autoregressive text introduces severe architectural failures. Robust system design requires an asymmetric training objective through selective loss masking, strictly confining gradient computation to the model's generated reasoning traces and executable action tokens while masking exogenous environment observations, tool returns, and user turns. In parallel, managing the hardware memory hierarchy requires balancing optimizer states against sequence-dependent activation footprints, necessitating the combination of parameter-efficient fine-tuning with activation checkpointing across long multi-turn sequences. Finally, offline validation loss and token perplexity fail to reflect closed-loop viability; empirical evaluation mandates executing the adapted policy within sandboxed runtime environments under identical latency constraints, tool failure modes, and execution budgets to verify true task completion.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Core Systems Principles of Supervised Policy Adaptation"}
1. *Trajectories are not plain text: enforce strict serialization of role boundaries and temporal causality.* Multi-turn agent trajectories interleave instructions, rationales, executable tool invocations, and environmental observations, requiring explicit schema tokens and strict serialization to prevent contextual boundary confusion during autoregressive generation.
2. *Action-targeted loss masking is mandatory: never compute gradients on environment observations.* Calculating cross-entropy loss over external tool outputs and user inputs forces the model to predict stochastic environment transitions, degrading policy calibration and penalizing valid interactions.
3. *LoRA mitigates optimizer memory but leaves activation memory untouched; plan for activation checkpointing.* Parameter-efficient adapters drastically reduce the static footprint of parameter weights and optimizer states, yet activation memory scales linearly with context length and batch size, requiring selective recomputation during long-horizon sequence training.
4. *Combat exposure bias through dataset aggregation (DAgger) and controlled fault injection.* Imitating pristine demonstration traces leaves agents vulnerable to compounding distribution shifts; injecting synthetic syntax faults, API failures, and perturbed trajectories into the training corpus conditions the policy to execute autonomous error recovery.
5. *Evaluate complete task completion under identical runtime limits, not validation perplexity.* Next-token prediction accuracy does not correlate with multi-step functional convergence, demanding closed-loop evaluation against executable environments with realistic timeouts, deterministic sandboxing, and stringent operational budgets.
:::

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From Supervised Adaptation to Environmental Reinforcement Learning"}
Supervised adaptation successfully teaches procedural discipline, interface syntax compliance, and foundational tool orchestration, but it remains fundamentally bounded by the quality, diversity, and distributional coverage of demonstrated paths. When agents encounter complex, non-stationary environments where optimal trajectories are unknown or human demonstrations are infeasible to collect, imitation learning cannot discover novel or counter-intuitive solution strategies. To navigate these high-dimensional state spaces autonomously, agents must transition from passive behavioral cloning to active trial, error, and optimization against objective task criteria. In Chapter 14 (*Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards*), we examine how agents learn directly from executable environmental feedback, analyzing policy gradient mechanisms, credit assignment across multi-turn tool interactions, and reward architectures derived from deterministic unit tests and formal verifiers.
:::

<!-- SUMMARY_END -->
